issues.detail: Covers the happy path and a few pitfalls (cyclic types, string.numeric not converting) but gives no guidance on unions of object types, handling of unknown or extra keys, async validation, or errors thrown by morphs.
The two examples are prose descriptions of what the agent does, with no runnable code or full input/output, so they are less realistic than the code blocks in the Instructions.

scenarios.name: express-body-validation-middleware
scenarios.rationale: Both responses define the schema with `type({...})`, `string.email`, `number.integer >= 13`, `bio?`, an `instanceof type.errors` check, a 400 response with `.summary`, and `typeof X.infer`. B adds structured details and an exported type, and it flags that it is untested. A adds a reusable factory and more usage notes, but its sample error text is presented as real output without being verified.

scenarios.name: zod-to-arktype-migration-with-coercion
scenarios.rationale: Both use string.email, the instanceof type.errors check, and type("string").pipe for tags; B uses string.integer.parse, which is not the rubric's string.numeric.parse but does parse the string to a number, and its answer is clean. A names string.numeric.parse as the rubric requires, but it leaves a stray duplicate type alias and a confusing note, and it admits it hasn't tested the pipe chaining.

scenarios.name: cyclic-user-post-scope
scenarios.rationale: A uses scope({...}).export() with optional back-references (posts?, author?) and checks instanceof type.errors, matching the rubric closely; B uses type.module instead of scope, makes the cyclic references required so it has to work around that with a hand-built finite nesting, though it does check instanceof type.errors.
